text:
When you type a web address, your browser has to find the server's IP address before it can load anything. That lookup is called DNS resolution, and it usually takes a fraction of a second.

The browser checks its own cache first, since it keeps the addresses of recently visited sites. If the address isn't there, the request goes to a recursive resolver, which does the lookup for you. The resolver asks a root server where to look. The root server points it to the right top-level domain server (.com or .org, for example), and that server points it to the authoritative server, which holds the site's actual address.

The resolver sends the address back to your device and keeps a copy for a while. A setting called TTL (time to live) controls how long it keeps that copy, often about 300 seconds. Until the copy expires, your next visit to the site skips the full lookup and loads faster.
